title: Knockaround Guys
full_review:
Four Brooklyn toughs, out to move higher up in the mob, find themselves in mortal jeopardy when they lose a bag of mob money in the steely drama "Knockaround Guys" (New Line).

Born into a Brooklyn mob family, Matt was taken at age 12 by his Uncle Ted (John Malkovich) to kill the goon that ratted on Matt's dad (Dennis Hopper). But Matt couldn't pull the trigger so never got far in the mob.

Now in his 20s, Matt (Barry Pepper) and his three buddies would like to move on up. Taylor (Vin Diesel) is violent enough but feels held back since he's half-Jewish, Chris (Andrew Davoli) is more of a ladies' man, and his cousin Johnny (Seth Green), a pilot of small planes, isn't too bright.

Dad and Uncle Ted reluctantly give Johnny a bag of mob money to fly to Spokane, Wash., but when he lands in Montana to refuel the bag is stolen by baggage handlers and the local sheriff (Tom Noonan) quickly gets the bag back -- and decides to keep it. Matt, Taylor and Chris fly in, but the sheriff is not intimidated by their threats.

Matters get grim when Uncle Ted and his goons arrive, determined to literally teach all involved a short-lived lesson.

Written and directed by David Levien and Brian Koppelman, the film's characters are all morally compromised if not downright evil. As such, the gutter language is continual and, when violence erupts, it's intense and ugly.

Yet for all its repelling aspects, the film can be seen as a cautionary tale: Those who opt for crime and greed are no better off for it; in fact, many end up face down in a pool of blood. The story also ends on a partially redemptive note as the key character changes the direction of his life, albeit escaping punishment for his past actions.

The narrative lags at times and is heavy on dialogue, but Malkovich is dependably creepy and Pepper convincing as the nephew wanting more of the action. Diesel wears the tough-guy role comfortably as well, but it is Noonan as the sheriff whose sly facial expressions really steal the show.

Due to brutal beatings and shootings, some profanity, constant rough language and brief drug abuse, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
